insider_note: The half-angle identity 1+cosθ=2cos²(θ/2) is the standard first move whenever a definite integral has √(1+cosθ) or √(2+2cosθ) under the root.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Rewrite using the half-angle identity
steps.margin_note: First mark. 1+cosθ = 2cos²(θ/2) is the identity that removes the square root cleanly.
lines: ∴ I = ∫₀^π √(4cos²(θ/2)) dθ = ∫₀^π 2cos(θ/2) dθ   [cos(θ/2) ≥ 0 on 0 ≤ θ ≤ π]
steps.why: Factoring out 2 and using 1+cosθ = 2cos²(θ/2) turns the square root into a plain cosine, because cos(θ/2) stays non-negative for θ between 0 and π so the square root of its square is itself.
common_mistakes: Using the identity 1 − cosθ = 2sin²(θ/2) by mistake.
Not checking the sign of cos(θ/2) before removing the square root.

steps.label: Integrate and apply the limits
steps.margin_note: Second mark. ∫cos(θ/2)dθ = 2sin(θ/2) + c — the 1/2 inside cos always doubles the outer factor.
steps.memory_tip: sin(π/2) = 1 is the standard value to remember here.
steps.why: Integrating cos(θ/2) gives 2sin(θ/2) by the reverse chain rule, and evaluating at θ=π gives sin(π/2)=1 while θ=0 gives sin0=0.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the extra factor of 2 that comes from integrating cos(θ/2) rather than cosθ.
Evaluating sin(π/2) incorrectly as 0 instead of 1.
